summary: Set the exact mechanism for the baseline account gate on review submission (Entry 16), and defined how it evolves over time without pre-committing to specific future restrictions.
context: Entry 16 established that a baseline gate exists on review submission from launch, with additional restrictions layered on as the platform grows, but left both the exact gate mechanism and the evolution process unspecified. A starting proposal was put forward for confirmation rather than treated as an open-ended question, consistent with how the numeric thresholds in Entry 29 were resolved.

options.name: Minimum account age only
options.description: Require an account to be a minimum number of days old before its first review. Simple, but doesn't verify the account is a real, reachable identity.

options.name: Email verification only
options.description: Require a confirmed email address before posting a review. Verifies a reachable identity but doesn't slow down a determined spammer who can verify instantly.

options.name: Email verification + minimum account age (combined)
options.description: Require both a confirmed email address and a minimum account age (e.g. 3 days) before the first review. Combines identity verification with a time delay that blocks the fastest throwaway-signup spam pattern, at low cost to genuine new users.

decision: The baseline gate requires email verification (mandatory) plus a minimum account age of 3 days before a user can submit their first review. For how the gate evolves over time, no specific future restriction is pre-committed: the Main Admin periodically reviews observed abuse signals (reports-per-day, spam-flagged review rate) and adjusts the gate's parameters through the admin config panel, since these values are stored as admin-configurable data rather than hardcoded.
rationale: User confirmed the proposal. The combined email-verification-plus-age gate balances low friction for genuine users against blocking the fastest spam pattern. Leaving the future evolution process open rather than pre-specifying restrictions avoids inventing hypothetical rules without real abuse data to justify them — the same reasoning already applied to deferring the recommendation engine's algorithm design (Entry 21).

title: Admin Trust Criteria for Lifting Review-Approval Requirement — Manual Case-by-Case
relatesTo: Resolves the first open sub-item from Entry 28
summary: Decided how the Main Admin determines when a non-founder admin is trusted enough that their reviews no longer require approval before publishing.
context: Entry 28 established the review-approval gate for non-Main-Admin admins but left open what criteria would trigger lifting that requirement for a given admin.

options.name: Automatic rule
options.description: E.g. the requirement lifts automatically after a fixed number of consecutive approved reviews. Removes subjectivity and scales without the Main Admin's attention, but an arbitrary numeric threshold doesn't necessarily reflect genuine trust, and requires building extra tracking/automation for a low-volume decision.

options.name: Manual case-by-case Main Admin judgment
options.description: The Main Admin decides individually, whenever they judge a given admin trustworthy enough, with no fixed rule. Simpler to build (no extra tracking logic), and fits a model where the Main Admin personally recruits and vets a small number of admins early on.

decision: No automatic rule — the Main Admin lifts the review-approval requirement for a given admin as a manual, case-by-case judgment call.
rationale: User confirmed the proposal. Given the Main Admin will likely personally recruit and vet a small number of trusted admins in the early stages, a manual judgment call better reflects genuine, considered trust than an arbitrary numeric threshold, and avoids building tracking/automation infrastructure for what is expected to be an infrequent, low-volume decision.

title: Confirmed — Unapproved Admin Reviews Are Not Visible or Votable Until Approved
relatesTo: Resolves the second open sub-item from Entry 28
summary: Confirmed the working assumption that an admin-authored review pending Main Admin approval is fully hidden from the rest of the platform until approved.
context: Entry 28 introduced the review-approval gate but left the visibility of a pending review as an unconfirmed working assumption rather than an explicit decision.
decision: An admin-authored review awaiting Main Admin approval is not published or visible to other users, cannot be voted on or commented on, and does not enter the seal-verification pipeline (Entry 6) until it is approved.
rationale: User confirmed. This is the only design consistent with the purpose of the review-approval gate in the first place — an unapproved review appearing publicly, or accumulating votes/seal candidacy, would defeat the requirement entirely.

title: WP0.1 Implemented — Next.js/Prisma Scaffold, with a Schema Correction and a Prisma 7 Adjustment
relatesTo: Implements Work Package WP0.1 from the Requirements Engineering doc, Section 8
summary: Scaffolded the Next.js/TypeScript app and Prisma schema per the chosen stack (Entries 30–39), and made two implementation-time decisions not previously spelled out: dropping the password_hash field from the User model, and adopting Prisma's driver-adapter pattern.
context: WP0.1 covers project scaffolding, the core data model, Supabase project setup, and Vercel's deploy pipeline. This entry covers what was actually completed: Next.js init (TypeScript, App Router, Tailwind, ESLint) at the repo root, Prisma init and a full schema.prisma translating Section 7's data model into models/enums, a seed script for the Category/SealType tables, and env-variable scaffolding (.env.example) for the Supabase variables Section WP0.2 will need. Supabase project creation and Vercel repo import were not completed in this step, since both require an interactive browser login only the user can perform.
decision: Two implementation-time refinements to the documented design: (1) The `User` model does not store a password_hash field, unlike the brief's original generic sketch — Supabase Auth (Entry 34) owns credentials and sessions entirely; the Prisma `User.id` is set to match the corresponding `auth.users.id` rather than being independently auto-generated, and the table only holds app-profile fields (username, avatar, bio, role, reputation, etc.). (2) Prisma 7's new 'prisma-client' generator (used per Entry 33) requires an explicit driver adapter rather than an implicit DATABASE_URL connection — `@prisma/adapter-pg` (node-postgres) was added and wired into both the app's Prisma singleton (src/lib/prisma.ts) and the seed script, since this wasn't yet known at the time Entry 33 was decided.
rationale: Both are corrections forced by details only visible once actually building against the chosen tools, not changes of direction: storing a redundant password_hash would contradict Entry 34's own reasoning (Supabase Auth as the single source of truth for credentials), and the driver-adapter requirement is simply how Prisma 7's client generator works — node-postgres is the standard, well-supported adapter for a plain Postgres connection (as opposed to Neon's or PlanetScale's specialized serverless adapters), so it was the natural choice given Entry 32's Supabase/Postgres decision.
openSubItems: Supabase project creation (WP0.2) — requires the user to sign up and create a project via the Supabase dashboard; connection details then go into .env per .env.example.

Vercel repo import — the user already has a Vercel account; the GitHub repo (sol-arcadedev/CertifiedBangers) still needs to be imported via the Vercel dashboard to stand up the deploy pipeline and Vercel Cron (Entry 36).

title: Title Catalog Sourcing — AniList Import as Primary, Manual Entry as Fallback
relatesTo: Revises WP1.2 (Requirements doc Section 8), which originally specified manual/admin-seeded titles only — README Section 9's MVP cut explicitly said "no scraping needed for MVP." That assumption is superseded by this entry.
summary: Titles are now primarily populated by importing from AniList's public API rather than typed in by hand. Manual entry stays available as a fallback for titles AniList doesn't have.
context: WP1.2 shipped with an admin panel where every title was hand-typed (name, alt names, genres, synopsis, cover upload, etc.). The user redirected this after WP1.2 and WP2.1–WP2.3 were already built: admin-typed metadata doesn't scale as a catalog-seeding strategy and duplicates work that reliable public manga/manhwa databases already do well — correct romanized/native/English titles, genre tags, synopses, cover art, and publication status, kept up to date by that source rather than by hand.

options.name: AniList
options.description: Free public GraphQL API, no API key or app registration required, generous rate limits. Its "MANGA" media type covers manga/manhwa/manhua together, distinguished by countryOfOrigin (JP/KR/CN/TW) and format (MANGA vs. ONE_SHOT vs. NOVEL), which maps cleanly onto this project's TitleType enum. Includes romaji/english/native titles, synonyms, genres, description, cover art, publication status, and staff credits.

options.name: MangaDex
options.description: Free API, no key required, manga/manhwa/manhua-focused with strong community-maintained metadata and cover art. Its terms of service are oriented around scanlation distribution, which sits closer to the content this project explicitly avoids hosting (brief Non-Goals: "not a scanlation/hosting site") — metadata-only use is likely fine but is a murkier fit than AniList's general-purpose media database.

options.name: Jikan (unofficial MyAnimeList wrapper)
options.description: Free, no auth required. Low rate limit (~3 req/sec, stricter than AniList's), and MAL's manga catalog is generally weaker on manhwa/manhua coverage than AniList's, since MAL's community and tooling historically skew toward Japanese media.

options.name: Manual entry only (status quo)
options.description: Keep WP1.2 exactly as built — every title hand-typed by an admin. Simplest to reason about and requires no external dependency, but doesn't scale catalog growth and duplicates data-entry work an existing free API already solves.

decision: Use AniList as the primary source: admins search AniList by name from the admin panel and import a match, which fetches its metadata and re-uploads its cover art to this project's own Supabase Storage bucket (not hot-linked from AniList) — consistent with the brief's cover-art approach (Entry 35). Manual entry (the existing WP1.2 form) stays as a fallback for the rare title AniList doesn't have, or for post-import corrections. A Title now carries an optional `anilistId`, null for manually created titles, so a title already imported can't be imported a second time.
rationale: User's explicit direction. AniList was chosen over the alternatives because it needs no registration/API key (lowest integration cost), its rate limits are comfortable for an admin-driven (not high-volume automated) import flow, and its data model already distinguishes manga/manhwa/manhua the same way this project's schema does. Keeping manual entry as a fallback — rather than removing it — avoids a hard dependency on AniList's catalog completeness; if a title genuinely isn't there, the admin isn't blocked.

title: Hidden Gem Seal Removed — Certified Banger Is Now the Only Seal Type
relatesTo: Revises Section 2.3 (Entries 14, 15, 29) and Work Packages WP4.3/WP5.1/WP7.3 from the Requirements Engineering doc.
summary: The Hidden Gem seal — a popularity-gated seal awarded to high-quality reviews on low-popularity titles — has been removed entirely, along with its popularity-gate logic, admin config entry, homepage/seals-page showcase section, browse-page filter checkbox, and card badge. Certified Banger is now v1's only seal type.
context: User direction, ahead of building a reputation/points system rewarding reviewing and voting, logged as a separate future entry. Hidden Gem existed as a discovery mechanism (Entry 15: a quality-gate-crossing review on a low-popularity title earned Hidden Gem instead of Certified Banger, and kept it permanently even after the title later became popular), but the user chose to simplify the seal system down to one clear signal rather than carry the dual-seal popularity split forward.
decision: Removed: the sealPopularityGateThreshold platform setting (its only purpose was choosing between Hidden Gem and Certified Banger); Title.hiddenGemCount and Title.totalSealCount columns (the latter was purely certifiedBangerCount + hiddenGemCount, now redundant with certifiedBangerCount alone — the "most seals" sort reads certifiedBangerCount directly instead); the Hidden Gem SealType seed row and its LOCKED_SEAL_TYPE_NAMES entry; checkAutoSealCandidacy's popularity-gate branch (src/lib/seal-probation.ts) — crossing the quality gate now grants Certified Banger directly, unconditionally; every UI surface showing a Hidden Gem badge, filter, or showcase section (homepage, /seals, /titles browse filters, title detail page, title card grid). The existing "Hidden Gem" SealType row and its one test SealAward were deleted from the live database (user's explicit consent — see below) rather than left as orphaned data, matching "remove completely."
rationale: User's explicit direction. Applying the schema change required prisma db push --accept-data-loss against the project's only Postgres database (the same Supabase instance backing the live Vercel deployment — no separate dev database exists). Prisma 7's CLI includes an AI-agent safety guard (PRISMA_USER_CONSENT_FOR_DANGEROUS_AI_ACTION) that blocks exactly this kind of destructive schema change from being run by an agent without the human explicitly reviewing and approving it first — consistent with Entry 43's prior note about this same guard. The user was asked directly (via a structured confirmation prompt, not inferred from the broader "remove Hidden Gem" request) whether to proceed with the column drops and whether to also delete the existing Hidden Gem SealType/SealAward rows, and approved both before the push ran. Separately, prisma db push hung indefinitely against the Supabase transaction-mode pooler (port 6543, used for the app's normal runtime queries since Supabase's direct connection is IPv6-only and unreachable from Vercel's serverless functions) because that pooling mode doesn't support the session-level advisory locks schema-push operations need; switching to the session pooler (same host, port 5432) for this one command let it complete in ~2 seconds.

title: Reputation System — Points for Reviewing and Voting
relatesTo: Implements the previously-unused User.reputationScore field (WP0.1, displayed on profile/admin pages since launch but never written to) — extends Section 2.4's "basic reputation indicator" requirement.
summary: User.reputationScore is now actually computed: +2 for each published review, +25 for each Certified Banger seal earned, net upvotes/downvotes received on your reviews, and +1 per vote cast on someone else's review (capped at 10/day). Recomputed from source data on every relevant event, not accumulated incrementally.
context: The reputationScore field has existed since WP0.1 and is already displayed on both the public profile page and the admin users list, but nothing ever wrote to it — every user showed 0. User asked for a system that rewards both writing reviews and voting on other people's reviews, ahead of which Entry 45 removed the Hidden Gem seal to keep the seal system (and by extension this points system) down to one clear quality signal.

options.name: Recompute from scratch on each event (chosen)
options.description: A recomputeUserReputation(userId) function reruns a handful of aggregate queries (published review count, net votes on those reviews, Certified Banger count, votes cast grouped by day) and writes the total, every time something relevant happens — same precomputed-aggregate-updated-incrementally-but-recomputed-fresh pattern already used for Title (Entry 39).

options.name: Incremental point deltas
options.description: Add/subtract a fixed delta at the moment each event happens (e.g. +1 reputation the instant an upvote is cast, -1 the instant it's removed). Cheaper per write, but every code path that creates/changes/deletes a Vote or SealAward has to remember to apply the exact correct inverse delta, and a missed or double-applied case silently drifts the score from what the underlying data actually implies — worse, it would need special-casing to stop the daily vote-cast cap from being trivially bypassed by undoing and redoing the same vote.

decision: Added src/lib/user-reputation.ts, wired into every place a user's counted activity changes: creating/editing a review (src/lib/actions/reviews.ts), a review's approval status changing (src/lib/actions/review-moderation.ts), a seal being granted or revoked whether by an admin (src/lib/actions/seals.ts) or automatically (src/lib/seal-probation.ts), and a vote being cast, switched, or undone (src/lib/actions/votes.ts) — recomputing both the review author's and the voter's reputation, since a vote affects both sides. Also added scripts/backfill-reputation.ts (npm run backfill:reputation) and ran it once against the live database so pre-existing reviews/votes/seals count retroactively instead of every user starting at 0.
rationale: User's explicit direction on the point values and mechanics (review: +2, Certified Banger: +25, net votes received: 1:1, voting engagement: +1/day capped at 10/day). Recomputing from scratch avoids an entire class of drift/double-counting bugs an incremental-delta design would need to guard against by construction, at the cost of a few more read queries per event — an acceptable tradeoff at this platform's scale, consistent with Entry 39's own reasoning for precomputed-but-recomputed Title aggregates.

title: Rating Categories Reduced to Four — Uniqueness Removed
relatesTo: Revises Entry 2 (original five-category seed) and Section 2.2 of the Requirements Engineering doc.
summary: The "Uniqueness" rating category was removed. Reviews are now rated across four categories: Art Style, Character Design, Story, Pacing. This also caught prisma/seed.ts up to two category renames (Character -> Character Design, Plot -> Story) made earlier this session directly against the live data, which the seed file had never been updated to match.
context: User direction. Categories are data-driven (Category table, Entry 2) specifically so this kind of change is a data operation, not a code change — but Uniqueness already had 17 real ReviewCategoryScore rows attached, across 17 published reviews on 11 titles, all on the platform's only Postgres database (same instance backing the live Vercel deployment, per Entry 45 — still no separate dev database).
decision: Deleted the 17 ReviewCategoryScore rows referencing Uniqueness, then deleted the Category row itself, then recomputed the affected 17 reviews' overallScore (the simple average of each review's remaining category scores, Entry 4) and the 11 affected titles' aggregates (avgCategoryScores/communityScore/reviewCount via the existing recomputeTitleAggregates, src/lib/title-aggregates.ts — no code changes needed there since it already derives everything from whatever categories currently exist). Also updated prisma/seed.ts's CATEGORIES array to the current four names, so a fresh install seeds the same set the live database now has, rather than reintroducing Uniqueness (and the two stale pre-rename names) on a future reseed.
rationale: User's explicit direction on removing the category. Recomputing overallScore/title aggregates after the deletion (rather than leaving them stale until the next unrelated review edit) follows the same 'never let a precomputed aggregate silently drift from source data' principle as every other aggregate in this codebase (Entry 39). Given the confirmed pattern from Entry 45 (destructive DB operations against the platform's only database go through explicit user confirmation, not an assumption that a broader request implies consent for the specific irreversible step), the user was asked directly — with the exact row/review/title counts affected — before the deletion ran, and approved.

title: Spoiler-Free Main Review Body, With a Separate Always-Collapsed Spoiler Field
relatesTo: Revises Entry 5's original spoiler_flag design (Section 2.2 of the Requirements Engineering doc, WP2.1).
summary: Review.spoilerFlag (a boolean toggle that hid the entire review body behind a click-to-reveal when checked) was replaced with Review.spoilerText, a separate optional field. The main review body must now stay spoiler-free by policy; any spoiler-specific commentary goes in the new field instead, which is always rendered collapsed by default purely because it has content — no flag to remember to check.
context: User direction: readers should be able to read any review's main text without risk of being spoiled, while still letting reviewers share spoiler-specific thoughts somewhere. The old spoilerFlag design hid the *entire* review (verdict included) behind a click if a reviewer checked one box, which didn't serve that goal — a spoiler-free reader still had to choose between skipping the review entirely or reading it and hoping the flag was set honestly.
decision: Schema: prisma/schema.prisma's Review model replaces spoilerFlag (Boolean) with spoilerText (String?, nullable). src/lib/actions/reviews.ts reads/stores it from the new spoilerText form field instead of a checkbox. src/components/review-form.tsx replaces the "Contains spoilers" checkbox with an optional "Spoiler details" textarea below the main review field, plus a small policy note directly under the main field: keep it spoiler-free, and reviews with unhidden spoilers in the main text will be removed. src/app/titles/[id]/page.tsx now always renders bodyText plainly, and separately renders spoilerText (when present) inside a collapsed <details> "Contains spoilers — click to show". Applied via prisma db push against the live database (0 of 17 existing reviews had spoilerFlag=true, so no real spoiler content was lost in the column drop — confirmed with the user before running it, per the Entry 45/47 precedent).
rationale: User's explicit direction on the mechanism. Dropping the boolean flag entirely (rather than keeping both a flag and the new field) avoids two overlapping ways to express the same thing — the new field's mere presence already fully implies "this needs to stay hidden," so a separate checkbox would be redundant and could drift out of sync with it. No automatic spoiler detection was built for the main body's no-spoiler policy — that's enforced the same way every other content policy on the platform is (the existing Report system plus human moderation), not a new automated feature.

title: Category Ratings Changed From a 1-10 Dropdown to a 5-Star Hover Widget
relatesTo: Revises Entry 2's original 1-10 numeric scale (Section 2.2 of the Requirements Engineering doc, WP2.1).
summary: Each category is now rated on a 1-5 star scale with a hover-to-preview widget instead of a 1-10 numeric dropdown. src/components/star-rating.tsx is fully generic (renders however many stars a category's scaleMin/scaleMax define, per Entry 2's data-driven design) rather than hardcoding 5 anywhere — the platform-wide change to 5 stars is a data change (each Category row's scaleMax), not a code change.
context: User direction. All four rating categories (Art Style, Character Design, Story, Pacing) were on a 1-10 scale.
decision: Added src/components/star-rating.tsx, a client component taking {name, min, max, defaultValue}: renders max-min+1 star buttons, hovering fills stars up to that index, clicking commits the value into a hidden input (a plain button has no native form value the way a <select> does). Swapped it into src/components/review-form.tsx in place of the old per-category <select>. src/lib/actions/reviews.ts needed no changes at all — its score validation already reads category.scaleMin/scaleMax dynamically, so it neither knew nor cared that the scale used to be 1-10. Rescaled the live data to match: each category's scaleMax changed from 10 to 5, each of the 17 existing ReviewCategoryScore rows converted via round(old/2) clamped to [1,5], then recomputed the 17 affected reviews' overallScore and the 11 affected titles' aggregates. Also updated prisma/seed.ts's and the admin CategoryForm's scaleMax defaults from 10 to 5 for consistency on fresh installs/new categories.
rationale: User's explicit direction on both the visual mechanism (stars, hover-fill) and the underlying scale (5, not 10). Building the widget scale-agnostically (rather than a component hardcoded to exactly 5 stars) keeps faith with Entry 2's original 'categories and their scale are data, not code' design — if a future category needs a different scale, the same component renders it correctly with no code change. Confirmed with the user before rescaling existing review data, per the Entry 45/47/48 precedent for destructive operations against the platform's only database.

title: Reviews Browse Page — a Dedicated Nav Item for Filtering Reviews Directly
relatesTo: Extends Section 2.7 (Discovery & Browsing) and WP5.1 with a review-centric counterpart to the existing title-centric /titles browse page.
summary: Added a "Reviews" nav item and /reviews page: the same search/genre/Format/Status filter bar as /titles, but browsing reviews directly instead of titles. Shows the most recent published reviews by default, narrowed by whichever filters are applied. Extracted the full-text title search helper (previously private to /titles) into src/lib/title-search.ts so both pages share it instead of duplicating the raw SQL.
context: User direction. Clarified during the build that the "content type" filter example (user said "Anime") meant Format (Manga/Manhwa/Manhua, the existing /titles Format filter) rather than a real new content type — this platform has no anime titles in its data model (README Non-Goals: manga/manhwa only in v1).
decision: A review has no independently searchable/filterable metadata of its own — genre, format, and status all live on its parent Title — so /reviews' filters (genre, Format, Status, and the same title full-text search as /titles) narrow the review list by joining through review.title. Reuses src/components/latest-reviews.tsx (previously homepage-only, showing a fixed 6 most-recent) for the review cards, now also driven by /reviews' filtered, larger (24) query. No sort dropdown was added — the page is explicitly “recent reviews, optionally filtered,” always ordered by createdAt desc, matching what was actually asked for rather than mirroring every /titles control.
rationale: User's explicit direction on the filter set (genre, format) and default-to-recent behavior. Extracting searchTitleIds into a shared lib file rather than copy-pasting it into the new page avoids two copies of the same full-text-search SQL silently drifting apart over time — the kind of duplication this codebase has consistently avoided elsewhere (e.g. Entry 39's shared aggregate-recompute functions).

title: Self-Service Avatar/Banner Upload and a Library Overview Stat on the Profile Page
relatesTo: Extends Section 2.4 (Users, Profiles) and WP1.1/WP5.2 with self-service profile customization.
summary: Profile owners can now upload their own avatar and banner image directly from their profile page, and a compact Library count stat was added alongside the existing Reviews/Reputation stats.
context: User direction. avatarUrl already existed on User (WP0.1) but had no upload UI anywhere — it could only ever be set by direct DB access. The profile page already showed a full library breakdown grouped by status, but had no compact at-a-glance count next to Reviews/Reputation.
decision: Added User.bannerUrl (nullable, additive column — no data-loss warning, so this one didn't need the Entry 45/47/48 destructive-change confirmation ritual). Created a new "profile-images" Supabase Storage bucket (src/lib/profile-image-storage.ts, extended scripts/setup-storage.ts) separate from title covers' "covers" bucket — avatars/banners split by path prefix within it since both are the same kind of thing (an owner-uploaded public image). src/lib/actions/profile.ts's updateProfileImages handles either or both files in one submission, re-uploading to this project's own storage (never accepting a raw URL) and deleting the old image first, same pattern as title cover uploads (Entry 35/44). src/components/profile-image-form.tsx renders inside a collapsed <details> ("Edit profile picture / banner"), shown only to the profile owner (src/app/profile/[username]/page.tsx now also fetches the current session user to compare). The banner renders as a full-width strip at the top of the profile with the avatar overlapping its bottom edge; a Library stat (count of all library entries, any status) sits next to Reviews/Reputation, above the existing per-status grids which stay as they were.
rationale: User's explicit direction on both features. Re-uploading to this project's own storage rather than accepting a hot-linked URL matches the exact reasoning already established for title covers (Entry 35) — no reason to relax that for user-uploaded images. A separate bucket (rather than reusing "covers") keeps content types cleanly separated by purpose, matching how this project already names things narrowly (COVER_BUCKET, not a generic "images" bucket).

title: Titles Are No Longer Imported — AniList Data Is Fetched Live, Always
relatesTo: Revises Entry 44 (AniList import as primary catalog source) and every WP1.2/WP5.1-descended piece of the title-browsing/search/admin surface.
summary: The platform no longer stores a persisted copy of AniList's title metadata (name aside, kept as a fallback) as its source of truth. Every AniList-linked title's genres, synopsis, author, status, scores, popularity, and favorites are now fetched live from AniList on every render, cached for an hour. Manual titles (AniList doesn't have them) are unaffected — still fully locally stored and admin-editable, since there's no other source for them.
context: User compared their Tower of God page against AniList's real page (screenshots) and found real mismatches: status showed "Ongoing" locally vs AniList's actual "Hiatus," plus drifted popularity/favorites/score. Root cause: Title rows copied AniList's metadata at import time; scripts/refresh-anilist-data.ts could refresh some of it but nobody ran it regularly, and it deliberately never touched status/genres/synopsis at all (those had admin-edit UI, and the script's design explicitly protected anything an admin might have manually corrected). User's direction: "I dont want any imported titles at all. All data for the titles and their metrics should be from anilist or wherever its free to fetch the data." Clarified during planning: everything AniList provides should go live (not just the fields that visibly drift); manual titles stay as a fallback; cover images keep re-hosting to Supabase Storage (a separate reliability decision, not part of the staleness problem).
decision: Schema stayed structurally unchanged (manual titles still need every column) — the change is behavioral. Three fields are still written and trusted locally, by deliberate exception: type (read synchronously on the review/library write paths for Category matching — a title's country-of-origin never changes, so it isn't "stale" the way status/scores are), and name/status (kept as a graceful-degrade fallback for when AniList is slow/unreachable at render time — a possibly-slightly-stale real name/status beats a generic placeholder, and a title's reviews are real local content that must stay visible regardless of AniList's uptime). Everything else is fetched live via two new src/lib/anilist.ts functions: getAniListMediaByIds (one batched AniList request for however many imported titles a page needs — required because AniList's public API is rate-limited to 30 req/min, confirmed live during planning) and getAniListGenreCollection (AniList's canonical genre list, replacing a local SELECT DISTINCT unnest(genres) query that no longer has data to distinct over). Both cached via Next's fetch revalidate (1 hour). src/lib/anilist-linked-titles.ts's hydrateWithLiveAniListData is the one shared primitive every list view (homepage Most Popular/Highest Rated, /titles and /reviews' genre/Format/Status/minScore filters, the admin titles list) uses to batch-fetch live data for a bounded "everything we've imported" set and filter/sort in-app, rather than trusting local columns or (for /reviews specifically) having no fallback at all. performAniListImport now only writes {anilistId, name, type, status, coverUrl} instead of copying every AniList field; scripts/refresh-anilist-data.ts (whose entire purpose was now moot) was deleted; a one-off migration (scripts/null-anilist-linked-metadata.ts, run against the live database with the user's confirmation) nulled the copied metadata on the 12 existing AniList-linked titles. Admin's manual title create/edit form (TitleForm) is now manual-titles-only; AniList-linked titles get a cover-replace-only form (CoverOnlyForm) instead, since there's nothing else local left to edit; the admin "possible duplicate" dedupe search now also checks AniList directly, not just local titles.
rationale: User's explicit direction on both the core ask and the three clarifying scope questions. The type/name/status caching exceptions were validated during planning (a dedicated Plan-agent review) as the minimal set actually necessary: type because Category-matching is a synchronous write-path dependency with no other reason to touch AniList, name/status because Postgres NOT NULL constraints on those two columns made a pure-live model impossible without a schema change, and turning that constraint into a deliberate resilience fallback (real cached data beats a generic placeholder when AniList is down) is strictly better than fighting it. The same review caught a genuine regression the original plan would have shipped: /reviews' genre/Format/Status filters had no AniList-blend fallback the way /titles does, so they would have silently returned zero results for almost every filtered query once local genre/status columns emptied out — fixed by extending the same live-hydration approach there. Batching (rather than one AniList call per title per render) is not an optimization here but a requirement, given the confirmed 30 req/min public rate limit.

title: Reader Activity Analytics on the Title Detail Page
relatesTo: Extends Section 2.5 (User Library) with a per-title library-status breakdown, previously only shown per-user on the profile page.
summary: Each title page now shows a Reader Activity section with counts of how many users have it as Currently Reading, Finished, Plan to Read, or Dropped in their library.
context: User direction. Clarified during the request: “paused” meant Plan to Read (haven't started), not a genuinely new fifth library status — the four existing LibraryStatus values (Entry 18/19) already cover what was being asked for, so no schema change was needed.
decision: src/app/titles/[id]/page.tsx groups LibraryEntry rows by status for the title (prisma.libraryEntry.groupBy) alongside its existing per-page data fetches, and renders a small card (only when at least one library entry exists) with one line per status. Read live on every render rather than precomputed — unlike Title's review-driven aggregates (Entry 39), library-status counts have no existing incremental-update hook anywhere library actions happen, and a single groupBy over one title's entries is cheap enough that adding one isn't warranted yet.
rationale: User's explicit direction, scope clarified before implementing to avoid building a fifth status nobody asked for. Kept as a live query rather than a new precomputed column since this data has no other consumer yet and the query is trivially cheap at a single title's scale — revisit as a precomputed aggregate only if this specific query is ever shown to be a real cost.

title: Follow System and Activity Feed
relatesTo: New v1 feature, extending Section 2.4 (Users, Profiles) with a social-graph layer not in the original brief.
summary: Users can follow other profiles. A new /feed page shows recent qualifying activity from people you follow: a published review, or a library status set to Finished or Dropped.
context: User direction: follow interesting profiles and see their activity in a feed. Clarified during planning that this meant a feed page to visit, not a persistent notification system with unread badges/read-state.
decision: Added a Follow model (followerId, followingId, unique compound key, indexed on followingId) with User back-relations `following`/`followers`. No new event-log table for the feed itself — a followed user's activity is derived live at feed-render time from the existing Review and LibraryEntry tables (same 'derive from source data' pattern as Reader Activity and the profile Library stat, Entry 53), rather than writing a new row on every qualifying review/library action. src/lib/actions/follows.ts's toggleFollow mirrors voteOnReview's toggle shape (create if absent, delete if present) and blocks following yourself. src/components/follow-button.tsx uses useOptimistic for an instant toggle. The profile page (src/app/profile/[username]/page.tsx) shows Followers/Following counts alongside the existing Reviews/Reputation/Library stats and renders the follow button next to the username when viewing someone else's profile while signed in. The new /feed page (requireUser-gated) merges published reviews and Finished/Dropped library entries from followed users, sorted by recency, with distinct empty states for 'following no one' vs 'no recent activity.' A 'Feed' nav link was added, shown only when signed in.
rationale: User's explicit direction on the core feature; the notification-mechanism question was clarified before implementing to avoid building unread-state/badge infrastructure nobody asked for. Deriving feed activity live rather than logging discrete events keeps this consistent with the rest of the app's aggregate/analytics features, at the accepted cost that a status change away from Finished/Dropped later erases that moment from the feed (LibraryEntry has no history, only current state) — a known, documented tradeoff rather than an oversight.

title: Hotfix: Homepage 500 When AniList Is Unreachable
relatesTo: Regression introduced by Entry 52 (live AniList data) — a gap the Plan-agent review that caught the /reviews regression didn't extend to the homepage/browse/admin-list hydration call sites.
summary: The homepage (and /titles, /reviews, the admin titles list) threw an uncaught error and 500'd whenever AniList's API was unreachable, because hydrateWithLiveAniListData's underlying batch fetch had no error handling at those call sites — unlike the title detail page and AniList preview page, which already degrade gracefully via .catch(() => null). Confirmed live: AniList's public API was actually down ("temporarily disabled due to severe stability issues", HTTP 403) when the user reported this.
context: User reported the homepage showing Next.js's generic error boundary ("Something went wrong"). Investigation found AniList's API was fully down at the time, and every page that calls hydrateWithLiveAniListData (src/lib/anilist-linked-titles.ts) — homepage Most Popular/Highest Rated, /titles and /reviews' genre/Format/Status/minScore filtering of already-imported titles, the admin titles list's unreviewed-sort view — had no fallback for that call throwing, unlike getAniListMediaById's existing .catch(() => null) pattern used on the title detail and AniList preview pages.
decision: Fixed at the shared primitive rather than at each of the four call sites individually: hydrateWithLiveAniListData now catches a failure from getAniListMediaByIds and degrades to "no live data for any row" (live: null for everything) instead of throwing — every caller already handles a null .live per-row (that's the not-yet-fetched/not-found case), so this required no changes at the call sites themselves. Also hardened getAniListMediaByIds itself to catch failures per-chunk rather than per-call, so a single failed batch (relevant once the catalog outgrows one 50-id request) doesn't discard results already fetched from earlier chunks.
rationale: A live external dependency (AniList) must never be able to take down a page that has its own valuable local content (reviews, aggregate scores) to show regardless of that dependency's uptime — the same principle already applied to the title detail page's graceful-degrade placeholder (Entry 52) evidently didn't get extended to the newer batch-hydration call sites added in the same effort. Fixing it once at the shared hydrateWithLiveAniListData primitive, rather than adding a try/catch at every current and future call site, makes this class of bug structurally impossible to reintroduce by a future caller forgetting to guard it themselves.

title: Full AniList Catalog Mirror, Refreshed Daily — Reversing Entries 44 and 52
relatesTo: Reverses Entry 44 (on-demand catalog growth) and Entry 52 (live-fetch, no local copy) after Entry 55's hotfix exposed the real cost of depending on AniList's uptime at render time.
summary: The platform now mirrors AniList's entire manga/manhwa/manhua catalog locally (same scope as before: type MANGA, format MANGA/ONE_SHOT, countries JP/KR/CN/TW) with full metadata and re-hosted cover images, refreshed once daily via a GitHub Actions scheduled workflow. Every render-time page reverted to plain local reads — no AniList API calls at page-render time at all, which also makes the platform fully immune to AniList outages (not just gracefully degraded, as Entry 55's hotfix achieved).
context: Following Entry 55 (a real AniList outage 500'd the homepage despite the Entry 52 architecture explicitly being designed around AniList's data), the user asked how much disk space a full local mirror would take (~10-15GB for cover images, metadata negligible), then decided to build it: 'we completely mirror all titles on anilist on our own db and let a script run periodically that updates the metric data for each title again from anilist... periodically in a reasonable timeframe.' Confirmed during planning: refresh cadence once daily, re-host every cover image (not hotlinked).
decision:
No schema changes — Entry 52 never dropped columns, only stopped trusting them for AniList-linked rows; this reverts to writing/reading them again. src/lib/actions/anilist-import.ts's performAniListImport writes full metadata again (on-demand import for the rare title not yet in the mirror). Every render-time page Entry 52 rewrote to live-fetch went back to plain `where`/`orderBy` local queries: src/app/titles/[id]/page.tsx (removed resolveTitleDisplay entirely), src/app/page.tsx (Most Popular/Highest Rated), src/app/titles/page.tsx and src/app/reviews/page.tsx (genre/Format/Status/minScore filters), src/lib/genres.ts and src/lib/title-search.ts (back to local-only queries), src/app/admin/titles/page.tsx (unreviewed-sort), and the admin title edit form (every title editable again, not just manual ones — deleted the now-unused CoverOnlyForm). src/lib/anilist-linked-titles.ts (Entry 52's shared live-hydration primitive) was deleted outright since nothing calls it anymore.

New sync infrastructure: scripts/lib/anilist-sync-shared.ts holds logic shared by both sync scripts (AniList request/retry, cover download/upload, concurrency-limited mapping, Media-to-Title-columns mapping) — self-contained from src/lib the same way scripts/seed-default-titles.ts already was (those files `import "server-only"`). scripts/mirror-anilist-catalog.ts is the one-time (but safely re-runnable) full backfill; scripts/refresh-anilist-catalog.ts is the recurring job (batch-refreshes every mirrored title's metadata, plus a newest-titles discovery pass), wired to run daily via .github/workflows/refresh-anilist-catalog.yml (GitHub Actions, not Vercel Cron — see rationale). Running the daily refresh requires DATABASE_URL/NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL/SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY as GitHub Actions repo secrets, which only the user can add.

A real bug was caught and fixed mid-build: a plain unfiltered AniList Page query caps out at ~5000 reachable results (page 100 at perPage 50), and pageInfo.total/hasNextPage/lastPage are unreliable above that ceiling — verified live against AniList's actual API. The mirror script partitions by publication start-year instead (each year's real count is safely under the cap) and treats an empty page, not hasNextPage, as the real end-of-results signal, with a warning log if any single year ever hits the page-100 ceiling (would need month-level sub-partitioning if that ever fires) plus an undated catch-all pass for titles with no publication date.
rationale: User's explicit direction, including the two clarifying choices (daily cadence, re-host every cover). GitHub Actions over Vercel Cron: a full-catalog refresh takes on the order of an hour or more even for a lightweight batched pass, which exceeds Vercel's serverless function timeout regardless of plan tier, while GitHub Actions' free tier allows up to 6 hours per scheduled job. The AniList pagination-cap bug was caught by actually running the script against the live API early and watching its real output rather than trusting the API's self-reported pageInfo fields — the same 'verify against reality, don't guess' discipline this project has applied to AniList's schema before (e.g. Entry 52's rate-limit discovery during planning).

title: Full AniList Catalog Mirror — Execution, Ceiling Fix, and Completion
relatesTo: Follow-up to Entry 56 (the full-mirror decision and initial scripts) — this entry covers actually getting the one-time backfill to run to completion.
summary: The one-time full-catalog backfill (scripts/mirror-anilist-catalog.ts) failed twice when run locally in the background (unrelated to the script — the local session/machine was interrupted mid-run), so it was moved to a new workflow_dispatch-only GitHub Actions workflow instead, which runs on a cloud runner independent of any local machine state. That surfaced two real bugs: the workflow initially specified Node 20, but @supabase/supabase-js's realtime-js dependency requires Node 22+ for native WebSocket support and crashed immediately; and AniList's ~5000-result ceiling (documented in Entry 56) turned out to apply per year too — years 2018-2025 each hit a hard error on page 101 partway through, silently truncating those years at ~5000 titles each. The mirror finished with 126,927 titles total after both a Node-version fix and a month-level sub-partitioning fallback for any year that hits the ceiling.
context: Entry 56 approved and built the mirror scripts and daily-refresh workflow; running the actual backfill was left as the final step. Two local background runs of the mirror script died partway through — the first after safely writing 1900-2004 (14,816 created), the second almost instantly on resume — with no error in either case, consistent with the local session/machine itself being interrupted rather than a script bug (real time had advanced several days mid-conversation). A multi-hour job needs a runner that survives independently of the developer's machine staying awake, which GitHub Actions provides.
decision: Added .github/workflows/mirror-anilist-catalog.yml (workflow_dispatch only, with start_year/end_year inputs so a re-run can target just the years that still need work instead of re-walking the whole catalog) and scripts/mirror-anilist-catalog.ts gained a START_YEAR/END_YEAR-aware year loop for the same reason. The first Actions run failed in ~5 seconds: createClient() from @supabase/supabase-js throws 'Node.js detected but native WebSocket not found' below Node 22 — both AniList-sync workflows (mirror and the existing daily refresh) were bumped from node-version: 20 to 22. The second Actions run reached year 2018 (~61k titles) before a page-101 HTTP 400 crashed the entire process — the script's per-page fetch is now wrapped so a single failed page logs and abandons just that year (or the undated pass) instead of taking down hours of accumulated progress, and a title that races into a 'unique constraint on anilistId' error (year-only FuzzyDateInt values like 20120000 satisfy two adjacent year ranges, so the same title can surface in two different year partitions) now falls back to an update instead of counting as a hard failure. The third Actions run completed successfully end to end (103,565 titles) but logged the page-101 ceiling for years 2018-2025 as a warning rather than an error, confirming those 8 years were each truncated. A new walkRange() helper is shared between the year-level pass and a month-level fallback: any year that hits the ceiling automatically re-walks itself month by month (comfortably under the per-query limit for a single year's manga release volume) instead of just logging a warning. A final targeted run (start_year=2018, end_year=2025) closed the gap cleanly with zero further ceiling hits at the month level, bringing the mirror to 126,927 titles.
rationale: Moving the one-time backfill to GitHub Actions follows the same reasoning Entry 56 already used for the recurring daily refresh (Vercel's function timeout can't hold a multi-hour job) — it turned out to apply to the initial backfill too, and more urgently, once local execution proved unreliable across session boundaries. Making page-level failures non-fatal rather than adding more retries was the right fix because the observed HTTP 400 was consistent and structural (AniList's actual server-side page-depth limit), not transient — retrying the identical request would only ever fail the same way, so the fix needed to change what the script does with an unreachable page, not how hard it tries to reach it. Verified end-to-end against the live API and the production database rather than assumed: each fix was confirmed by re-running the actual workflow and checking real row counts before moving to the next one.
